tei:titleStmt.tei:title: תחנה אמהות
Teḥinah Imahot for Shabbat Mevorkhim by Leah Horowitz in its original Aramaic (ca. 1790)

tei:div.tei:head: Teḥinah Imahot for Shabbat Mevorkhim by Leah Horowitz in its original Aramaic (ca. 1790)

tei:lg.tei:l: Yahh, master of the world and all worlds,
in six days you created
the heaven, the earth and everything residing therein
with ten pronouncements.
And on the seventh day you ceased from all speech.
You commanded the holy nation
that they should refrain from all talking
except for that concerning matters of heaven
and the hidden secrets;
and that the unlearned and the women, in their homes,
should consider in colloquial language
their obligations under the commandments.
Moreover, you gave us holidays for rejoicing
and new moons for remembrance.
When we were in Jerusalem the beautiful city,
the location of the residence of our Mother, the Shekhinah, in all its beauty,
the leaders of the people would sanctify [the new month] according to what they saw.
Now, in exile, the only thing left for us is to bless the new moon.
A time of grace; the time of blessing the new moon is here.
We spread our hands to our merciful Father in heaven,
return to us as in days of yore;
for ‘the strength of the labourers has failed’,
[we are] as a tender kid at the hottest part of the day.
Our joy, our holidays, our new moon festivals have gone.
We are like orphans with no father;
like sheep without a shepherd.
‘The enemy laid hands on all her treasures’
‘with no one to say: “Restore them!”’.
‘El of vengeance! Hashem, appear from Mount Paran.’
He who answered our fathers
will answer us this month
by the merit of the mountains of old and the hills.
Sarah, concerning whom you ordered,
‘Touch not my anointed ones!’ (Psalms 105:15):
indeed all who touch her descendants will be silenced.
Rivqah, whose blessing you imparted to us:
indeed soon will it be fulfilled.
Raḥel, whom you promised,
‘The children will return to their land’ (Jeremiah 31:16);
speed our return for her sake.
Léah, who had weak eyes
that she not be fated to be with the wicked one;
by her merit brighten eyes from the darkness of exile.
Innocent dove,
the sword drinks its fill,
crushed and violated the whole day long.
Daughter of our father Avraham;
fallen daughter of the exile;
daughter of our father Avraham
dwelling under harsh masters.
This one says, ‘Strike her!’
and that one says, ‘Me too!’
Wash us thoroughly
because we have already been doubly lashed for our disobedience,
and renew and bring us this month for joy;
that days and months change from ill to well.
Pride of our strength,
give us strength.
Dower us with a bountiful gift,
free of trouble and distress;
by the merit of Yaaqov, choice among the Patriarchs,
by virtue of his merit increase the good.
You called us, ‘my treasure’;
we called you, ‘my beloved’.
We pray to you a prayer that you will grant us,
and to all sages of the scholarly fellowship, holy scribes,
as well as those who present prayers and supplications,
male children, from the upper world, from the right side,
scholars of Torah, doing the will of our beloved in heaven,
with the utmost reverence and love;
like Mosheh, the faithful shepherd,
the beloved son of the supernal father and mother.
Amen, let it be his will.

tei:note.tei:p: Mishnah Avot 5:1, and many other places in rabbinic literature.

‘If you call the sabbath “delight”, the Lord’s holy day “honoured”; and if you honour it and go not your ways, nor look to your affairs, nor speak idly [daber davar]’ (Isa. 58:13). Various rabbinic sources interpreted this to mean that talking on the sabbath should be minimized or directed only to holy subjects (e.g. BT Shab. 113a; JT Shab. 15:3; Vayikra rabah, 34; Yalkut shimoni, ‘Isaiah’, 496).

The phrase, nashim ve’amei ha’arets (women and unlearned men), first appeared in BT Meg. 18a, in the context of people who did not understand the text of Esther when it was read publicly on Purim. By the Middle Ages this phrase had become a cliché denoting those who do not understand Hebrew and are not conversant with learned texts. See M. Rosman, ‘The History of Jewish Women in Early Modern Poland: An Assessment’, Polin, 18 (2005), 44–46.

Rashi and other medieval authorities emphasized that ‘women and unlearned men’ should be provided with translations in their own vernacular so that they could understand the commandments (Rashi on BT Meg. 21b). Here Leah substitutes lishna kelilya (‘easy’ or ‘colloquial’ language), for la’az (‘vernacular’; lit. ‘language of a foreign nation’), but in essence she is continuing the assertion that unlearned people also need to understand their religious obligations. See Yiddish Tkhine, Section M.

See Num. 10:10. Leah apparently understood the central passage of the musaf prayer service for Rosh Ḥodesh thus: ‘You have given your people new moon festivals as a time of atonement for all their generations. They would sacrifice before you loving sacrifices and sin-offerings to make atonement. [May our current Rosh Ḥodesh celebrations] be a memorial for all of these.’ For Leah, the core significance of the new moon festival in post-Temple times was to recall the service of the Temple; hence she averred: ‘and new moons for remembrance’.
Neh. 4:4
Cf. Ps. 94:1; Deut. 33:2; Yalkut shimoni, ‘Psalms’, 849.
This is an allusion to the blessing Moses gave to the tribe(s) of Joseph (see Deut. 33:15; cf. Ephraim Solomon of Luntshits, Keli yakar (Lublin, 1602), ‘Vezot haberakhah’).

This cataloguing of the merits of the matriarchs as the basis for Israel deserving divine favour is a standard trope in tkhines (see NLI R8°894501: Eyn gor sheyne tkhine; cf. the various tkhines in Klirs et al. (eds.), The Merit of Our Mothers; see also n. 102 below).
God did not allow either Pharaoh (Gen. 12:17) or Avimelekh (Gen. 20:3) to touch Sarah (cf. Yalkut shimoni, ‘Psalms’, 863; see Yiddish Tkhine, Section O).

This is the blessing Rebecca received from her mother and brother: ‘O sister! May you grow into thousands of myriads; may your offspring seize the gates of their foes’ (Gen. 24:60). Compare the blessing associated with Rebecca (Yiddish Tkhine, Section O) and analysis below.
According to Bereshit rabah, 70, Leah’s eyes were weakened by her copious weeping at the prospect that she might wind up having to marry Esau (‘the wicked one’).
Cf. Isa. 34:5.

Calling Israel the daughter of Abraham is a rare metaphor in classic Jewish texts (see Shir hashirim zuta, 7:2; Tseror hamor, ‘Bemidbar’ (lemma: beshem); see also Yiddish Tkhine, Section O; Liberman, ‘“Tkhine imohos”’, 437).
Both temples were destroyed.
See Bereshit rabah, 76; cf. Yalkut shimoni, ‘Vayishlah’, 131; ‘Psalms’, 865.
Heb.: segulati (see Exod. 9:5; Deut. 7:6; 14:2; 26:18; Mal. 3:17).
According to rabbinic tradition the term dodi (‘my beloved’), which appears repeatedly in the Song of Songs, refers to God.
On the preference for male children, see Fram, My Dear Daughter, 40–41.
In many cultures the right is associated with positive characteristics and the good in general (e.g. dexterous), while the left is associated with the negative and evil (e.g. sinister).

This is a precis of a theme in the zoharic work Ra’aya meheimna, where Moses the ‘faithful shepherd’ (ra’aya meheimna) is the son of his divine father and mother who represent respectively [the sefirot of] wisdom (ḥokhmah) and understanding (binah). My thanks to Daniel Abrams for pointing this out to me.
